growth_story.headline: Cuba's income per person collapsed in the 1990s, recovered strongly, then stalled after 2016; in 2024 it was about where it first was in 2013.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Cuba's income per person has grown in four eras: -3.4 percent a year in 1990–1998, 6.0 in 1999–2007, 2.8 in 2008–2015 and -0.4 in 2016–2024. The first era began with a collapse: the fall of the Soviet bloc ended Cuba's preferential trade and aid, and income per person fell every year from 1990 to 1993, by 15.3 percent in 1993 alone. Limited market reforms in 1993–94 came before a strong recovery in 1994–96, but a World Bank study says reform was virtually halted in 1996. The sources found say little about the fast growth of 1999–2007, which reached 11.9 percent in 2006, or the slower years to 2015, beyond a 2016 study's note that Venezuela sold oil to Cuba on heavily subsidized terms. Since 2016 growth has averaged -0.4 percent a year, against 4.1 in 2006–2015; income per person peaked in 2019, fell 10.7 percent in 2020, and by 2024 was 9.1 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 2013. Recent sources describe many Cubans leaving and, in October 2025, severe hurricane damage, but they say little about what caused the slowdown itself.

threads.title: Soviet aid ends
threads.text: The collapse of socialism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe ended the preferential trade and generous aid Cuba had relied on. Income per person fell in each year from 1990 to 1993, and the 1990–1998 era averaged -3.4 percent a year.

citations.title: Achievement and Deterioration of Universal Access to Social Services in Cuba
citations.quote: The collapse of socialism in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe ended the preferential trade relations and generous aid Cuba enjoyed from those countries.

citations.title: The Fall and Recovery of the Cuban Economy in the 1990's: Mirage or Reality?
citations.quote: The collapse of the Cuban economy following the cessation of Soviet assistance gave way to a strong recovery in 1994-96.

threads.title: Timid reforms, then a halt
threads.text: Cuba answered the crisis with an adjustment program and market-oriented reforms in 1993–94, which a World Bank study calls timid next to those of other socialist economies. A strong recovery followed, with income per person up 7.5 percent in 1996, but reform was virtually halted that same year.

threads.title: Subsidized oil from Venezuela
threads.text: Venezuela shipped part of its oil abroad on heavily subsidized terms, and a 2016 Growth Lab study of its oil industry names the bilateral deal with Cuba as the most important of these. The study does not measure what the deal meant for Cuba's growth.

threads.title: Cubans leave in large numbers
threads.text: Many Cubans have left during the slow era. Cuban asylum seekers in the United States reached decades-high numbers in 2022 and were still among the largest groups in 2023, and sending money home from the United States to Cuba grew more costly.

citations.title: International Migration Outlook 2024
citations.quote: Arrivals from Cuba, which were at decades-high levels in 2022, fell by 37% in 2023.

citations.title: International Migration Outlook 2024
citations.quote: Nevertheless, with over 99 000 applicants, Cubans were still the third top nationality of asylum seekers in the United States in 2023.

citations.title: Migration and Development Brief 38: Remittances Remain Resilient but Are Slowing

threads.title: Foreign investment in services
threads.text: Foreign firms have put new projects into Cuba. Leaving out Guyana, the OECD and IDB rank Cuba second only to the Dominican Republic among Caribbean destinations for greenfield foreign investment over 2014–2024, and across the region this money went mostly to services such as accommodation and food.

citations.title: Caribbean Development Dynamics 2026: Investing in Sustainable and Resilient Development
citations.quote: the Dominican Republic accounting for USD 18 billion (46% of the total), followed by Cuba with USD 7 billion (19%)

citations.title: Caribbean Development Dynamics 2026: Investing in Sustainable and Resilient Development
citations.quote: Greenfield FDI targeted predominantly the services sector, including accommodation and food, information and communication technology, and financial services

growth_story.tension: The OECD and IDB count Cuba among the largest Caribbean destinations for greenfield foreign investment over 2014–2024, yet the data record net foreign investment inflows of 0.0 percent of GDP.
